study_identification_part.si4_title: Dissecting Heterogeneity in Functional Network Connectivity Aberrations in Antipsychotic Medication-Naïve First Episode Psychosis Patients - A Normative Modeling Study

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To characterize inter-individual heterogeneity in functional networks in antipsychotic medication-naïve first-episode psychosis patients using normative modeling, and to investigate if normative values can be leveraged to identify biologically less heterogeneous subgroups of patients.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (standard deviations from normative reference); binarized using cut-off of ±2 standard deviations to define significant deviation; deviation load calculated (number of absolute, positive, and negative deviations per individual)
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper clearly describes the deviation metrics used, including z-scores, the binarization threshold, and the calculation of deviation loads.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: We quantified functional connection deviations expressed as standard deviations (z-score) from the normative reference range for each patient. We binarized z-scores to operationally define a significant deviation using a cut-off value of ±2 standard deviations. We then calculated connectivity deviations between the functional connections and calculated the deviation load (number of absolute, positive, and negative deviations in an individual patient)

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Statistical analyses to characterize heterogeneity: percentage of patients sharing the same functional connection deviations calculated; deviation load scatter plots created (negative vs positive deviations). Post hoc analyses: patients grouped into four theoretically-based deviation profiles (positive only, negative only, mixed, none); deviation patterns mapped for each subgroup with FDR correction (α=0.05); significance threshold for total deviations set at 4 or greater [136 connections × 0.025 one-tailed alpha = 3.4, rounded to 4]; z-tests used to compare subgroup heterogeneity (maximum patient similarity percentage within subgroups) against overall group maximum similarity; clinical characteristics (BPRS, RBANS) and cannabis use compared across subgroups using ANOVA and chi-square tests.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Functional network deviations in first-episode psychosis patients are highly heterogeneous, with no more than 11.1% of patients sharing deviations in the same connections; 48% of patients showed no significant deviations; subgrouping by deviation profiles (positive only, negative only, mixed, none) revealed biologically less heterogeneous subgroups that did not differ clinically.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study found that functional network connectivity deviations in 108 antipsychotic medication-naïve first-episode psychosis patients were highly heterogeneous at the individual level. No more than 11.1% of patients shared positive deviations in the same network connection, and no more than 8.3% shared negative deviations. Approximately 48% of patients had no significant functional connection abnormalities (using ±2 SD threshold). Among the 52% with significant deviations, 25% had exclusively positive connectivity deviations, 24% had exclusively negative deviations, and only 2.8% had mixed deviations. The positive deviation group showed up to 40.7% similarity in shared deviations (z=3.66, p=0.0001), most commonly in SM-A network connectivity to DAN-A, CCN-C, C. Visual network, DMN-A, and CCN-C networks. The negative deviation group showed up to 23.1% similarity (z=-2.15, p=0.016), most commonly in connections between SM-A and Limbic A network. Importantly, these biologically-defined subgroups did not differ in clinical presentation (BPRS total, positive, and negative symptom scores), cognition (RBANS scores), or cannabis use, demonstrating that normative modeling can identify neurobiologically distinct subgroups within a clinically homogeneous patient population.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Normative models likely overrepresent individuals with European ancestry and do not match patient demographics (63.89% racial/ethnic minorities); transferring model to diverse data should be done with caution; study limited to cortical functional networks (subcortical connectivity not examined); findings need independent replication; stability of subtypes over illness progression unknown
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: The normative models used here likely overrepresent individuals with European ancestry, which do not match our patient demographics. Prior studies suggest that transferring the model to diverse data should be done with caution. We acknowledge this as a major limitation given that many of the patients in this study identify (63.89%) as a racial/ethnic minority, a group that has historically lacked equitable inclusion in research studies... it is important to note that our investigation only included cortical functional networks. It remains unknown if this subtype is characterized by subcortical rather than cortical functional connectivity pathology... it will be important to independently replicate this finding in a different group of first-episode psychosis patients and to determine how stable these subtypes are as the illness progresses.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Patients were grouped into four theoretically plausible subgroups based on deviation profiles to test if subgroups exist in experimental data and whether they are less heterogeneous than the overall group. This theory-driven subgrouping approach was motivated by inconsistent literature showing only increased, only decreased, or mixed connectivity patterns. The study demonstrated that all four theoretical subgroups exist in real data and are neurobiologically more homogeneous despite being clinically indistinguishable.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a medRxiv preprint (not peer-reviewed). The study represents the first application of normative modeling to resting-state functional connectivity in antipsychotic medication-naïve first-episode psychosis patients. A major strength is the large medication-naïve FEP sample (N=108), which mitigates confounds of medication effects and illness chronicity. Cannabis users were not excluded to maintain generalizability. The finding that 48% of FEP patients show no significant functional connectivity deviations challenges conventional understanding of psychosis pathophysiology. The study used a pre-trained normative model with local calibration but did not validate model performance metrics. Race/ethnicity data shows 63 African American, 39 Caucasian, 4 Asian, 1 Hispanic/Latino, and 1 Other in the patient group. Supported by NIMH grants R01MH118484 and R01MH113800.
